title: Transparent headroom accounting and granular KV scheduling for GPU memory budgeting
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Design and implement a transparent GPU memory headroom accounting layer combined with a granular KV cache scheduler. The goal is to provide deterministic memory budgets across weights, KV cache, and activations while enabling continuous batching to operate without surprising OOMs or conservative over-provisioning. This ticket captures design decisions, APIs, telemetry needs, and an implementable rollout plan that minimizes customer disruption.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime exposes per-tenant memory ledger with separate counters for weights, KV, and active activations
Scheduler can evict or soft-preempt KV entries by priority bands and tenant-declared SLAs
Continuous batching throughput remains within 5% of baseline for typical chat workloads after enabling headroom accounting
No new P0 OOM incidents in the canary fleet for 2 weeks after rollout
Console surface shows token-level cost and headroom usage for at least 90% of requests in sampled traces
design_notes: Motivation: Current heuristics allocate a large static safety buffer to avoid OOMs when KV spikes or batched activations align. This wastes GPU slots and increases cost for dedicated customers.

Proposal: Introduce a transparent ledger that tracks committed weight residency, soft-reserved KV budget, and ephemeral activation allocations. Each incoming request computes a tentative memory delta and consults the ledger for headroom availability before entering the batching queue.

KV scheduling: Organize KV entries into priority tiers (hot, warm, cold) with a recency/utility score. Eviction favors cold entries and admits admissions based on available soft headroom. The scheduler supports per-tenant QoS hints: prefer preserving hot KV for low-latency customers, while bulk ingestion tenants accept higher eviction rates.

Interaction with continuous batching: Batch admission must be aware of the aggregate activation cost of the batch. Use a greedy bin-packing heuristic that prefers batches whose summed activation delta fits remaining headroom; if none, allow controlled incremental batching at lower batch sizes with a fast-fail fallback to a lower-cost model variant.

Headroom policy: Implement two bands — soft headroom (reclaimable via progressive KV eviction) and hard headroom (must not be exceeded; triggers backpressure). Soft headroom gives probabilistic guarantees; hard headroom enforces strict admission control.
Backward compatibility: Default behavior initially mirrors current heuristics. New accounting toggled via runtime flag per fleet to allow canary testing. API surface for tenant QoS hints is opt-in.

Memory accounting units: Use bytes with micro-buckets by allocation type. Maintain lightweight atomic counters to avoid contention on hot paths. Periodic reconciliation job fixes drift between simulated allocations and actual GPU residency.
Telemetry: Export both raw counters and derived signals (headroom utilization ratio, eviction rate by tier, batch-admission failures) to Console for visualization and automated alerts.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): Prototype ledger module in simulation harness; add unit tests for allocation/deallocation and eviction invariants.
Phase 2 (3 weeks): Implement ledger kernel in serving runtime (C++/CUDA fast path) with atomic counters and a light admission API; add scheduler hooks to batching path.
Phase 3 (2 weeks): KV tiering engine in user-space service with eviction policies and tenant QoS mapping; integrate with ledger soft-headroom reclaim path.
Phase 4 (1 week): Observability — export Prometheus metrics and Console traces; build initial dashboard.
Phase 5 (2 weeks): Canary rollout to internal and select low-risk customers; collect telemetry and iterate on thresholds.
Phase 6 (ongoing): Gradual expansion, safety polish, and postmortem if any incidents occur.
risk_and_mitigation: Risk: Ledger atomics may introduce contention on very high QPS paths. Mitigation: use sharded counters per worker and reconcile periodically; hot path reads use relaxed ordering.

Risk: Eviction spikes may increase tail latency for some queries. Mitigation: prioritize graceful degradation — serve smaller batches or fall back to cheaper model variants with clear telemetry marking.
Risk: Accounting drift causing false-headroom leading to OOM. Mitigation: fast reconciliation loop and hard-headroom enforcement; canary enables quick rollback.
Risk: Tenant UX confusion around opt-in QoS hints. Mitigation: document defaults, add examples, and provide recommended QoS templates in Console.
Risk: Metrics volume growth from fine-grained counters. Mitigation: aggregate at ingestion and expose summarized signals to Console; raw counters kept at low retention only for debug windows.
telemetry_and_metrics: ledger.headroom.soft_ratio (gauge) — fraction of soft headroom used per GPU
ledger.headroom.hard_ratio (gauge) — fraction of hard headroom used per GPU
kv.eviction.rate (counter) — evictions per minute per tenant and tier
batch.admit.failure.count (counter) — number of batch admissions failed due to headroom
batch.size.histogram — distribution of actual batch sizes post-admission
oom.incidents (counter) — OOMs attributable to accounting failure; must stay at 0 during canary
rollout_strategy: Start with a shadow mode that computes ledger decisions but does not enforce them; compare predicted admits with current behavior for 48 hours.
Enable enforcement on an internal canary fleet (10% of serving nodes) for 7 days; observe rollback signal thresholds: >1 P0 OOM or >20% increase in 95p latency for affected tenants.
Gradually widen to a 30% subset of low-risk customers with SLA tolerances, then to all dedicated nodes after 2 weeks of stable metrics.
Expose a runtime flag per-tenant to disable admission control for emergency support and for dedicated customers during migration windows.
Final step: default enforcement for new runtime versions; provide migration docs and Console toggles for existing customers.
testing_plan: Unit tests for ledger increments/decrements, eviction ordering, and reconciliation logic
Load tests with synthetic chat workloads across distribution of sequence lengths to measure batch admission failure rates
Chaos test: simulate KV storm by inflating KV writes and verify eviction and headroom reclamation behavior
Canary A/B: compare latency, throughput, and cost-per-token between baseline and ledger-enabled nodes
Regression tests ensuring no change in model output; validate deterministic fallbacks and model-variant routing under admission pressure
